Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman sent out a tweet with seemingly deliberate ambiguity in its wording, sparking quite a bit of discussion. Some have interpreted it as a hint that the iPhone event will be presented live on stage rather than via pre-recorded video.

Although the odds may be slim, there are still a few reasons to expect this year's live segments to be more energetic than in the past……

From on-stage launches to a hybrid format

Apple's launch events and iPhone reveals have traditionally been delivered live on stage. During the pandemic, Apple was forced to abandon the live format in favor of pre-recorded video for WWDC 2020, and the company was clearly happy enough with the result that it has stuck with pre-recorded video for both the WWDC keynote and iPhone events ever since.

Of course, live audiences have since returned, paired with Apple executives taking to the stage in person to introduce some of the pre-recorded segments, making for a hybrid experience. Personally, I think this is the best of both worlds: you get the audience reaction and stage presence, but with smoother flow and pacing for the presentation.

This year at WWDC, we saw Apple take the hybrid format one step further, holding a live Tech Talk discussion session immediately after the keynote.

  • Apple explains why the Siri iOS 27 overhaul took so long
  • Craig Federighi explains why Apple ultimately decided to ship a Siri chatbot app

On the phrase "in person"

Gurman subsequently published a piece about a lottery for retail employees to attend the event, with similarly conspicuous gaps in the tweet's wording.

Many have read the phrase "in person" as referring to a live keynote. In reality, there have always been Apple employees on the ground handling event operations, including managing queues, guest check-in, wayfinding, and assisting with hands-on sessions. That's almost certainly what's meant here.

Not a fully live event, but a livelier one

Some have suggested that with John Ternus taking over from Tim Cook at the helm, the event format could see major changes, but personally I suspect the opposite is more likely. Live presentations always carry the risk of demo failures or other mishaps, and for Ternus, going live for his first appearance as CEO would be a huge gamble.

That said, I do think this year's live segments will be more vibrant, for two reasons.

First, the iPhone Ultra is set to be one of the most significant changes to the iPhone lineup since the introduction of the iPhone X. If Apple holds an in-person discussion session after the video release, as it did at WWDC, the atmosphere on the ground is bound to be electric. With the new device officially unveiled, the company will also have more freedom to talk about its implications for iOS 27 and future versions.

Second, Ternus's style is noticeably more relaxed and natural than Cook's. That quality would lend a very different feel to a live discussion session or to informal interactions with attendees during hands-on sessions.

What do you think? Do you reckon we'll see a genuinely live keynote, or will Apple stick with its current hybrid format but with a bit more of a human touch? Feel free to vote and share your thoughts in the comments.
